reason: There are 20 well-documented claims supported by at least two sites explaining the physics of free fall and the biological impacts of weightlessness.
story: Most people think space is a gravity-free zone, but that’s a myth. At the International Space Station’s altitude, Earth’s gravity is still roughly 90% as strong as it is on the ground. Astronauts feel weightless because they and their spacecraft are in a state of perpetual free fall. The station moves sideways so fast that as it falls toward the planet, the Earth’s surface curves away beneath it. This means the crew is effectively falling around the world every 90 minutes. Because everything falls together, there is no floor pushing against their feet to create the sensation of weight. This constant falling causes body fluids to rush to the head, creating a puffy 'moon-face.' To stay healthy, astronauts follow strict exercise routines using specialized machines to prevent their muscles from wasting and their bones from turning as brittle as if they had osteoporosis.
angle: Gravity on the International Space Station is still 90% as strong as it is on Earth; astronauts only float because they are in a state of constant, high-speed free-fall around the planet.

claims.claim: Gravity is defined as the force that attracts two bodies and exists everywhere in the universe.
At the altitude of the International Space Station, Earth's gravity is roughly 90% as strong as it is at the surface.
Astronauts experience weightlessness because they and their spacecraft are in a continuous state of free fall.
Orbit is a balance between an object's forward motion and the pull of gravity.
Weight is the subjective experience of muscles resisting the pull of gravity or a support force pushing back.
The International Space Station completes one full orbit around Earth approximately every 90 minutes.
Space adaptation syndrome, or space sickness, affects nearly half of all people who travel into space.
In microgravity, body fluids shift toward the chest and head.
Headward fluid shifts cause a typical 'moon-face' or puffy appearance in astronauts.
Prolonged weightlessness causes muscles to atrophy and bones to lose mineral density.
Astronauts use handholds and foot loops on the interior of the spacecraft to keep from drifting.
Parabolic aircraft flights, nicknamed 'Vomit Comets,' simulate weightlessness for astronaut training.
Without a consistent support force, liquids in space form floating spheres.
Isaac Newton described the mathematical principles necessary to explain weightlessness and orbital motion.
Bone density loss in space is compared to the effects of osteoporosis.
Astronauts use tethers during spacewalks to ensure they do not float away from the spacecraft.
Space sickness symptoms include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and headaches.
Gravity prevents satellites and the ISS from flying off into deep space.
The inner ear's vestibular system becomes confused in space because it cannot identify 'up' or 'down'.
Muscle atrophy begins within the first few days of being unloaded in weightlessness.

disputed: The exact percentage of astronauts suffering from space sickness is 45 percent according to one source and nearly half according to others; the script should use 'nearly half'.

The altitude of the ISS is listed as 100-200 miles by one source and 400 kilometers by another; the script should attribute measurements to specific agencies or focus on the shared gravity percentage.
